content: Mercury(II) oxide exhibits a red or orange coloration. At standard room temperature and pressure, it exists as a solid. The red form of mercury(II) oxide (HgO) can be synthesized by heating elemental mercury (Hg) in the presence of oxygen at approximately 350°C. Alternatively, it can be produced through the pyrolysis of mercury(II) nitrate [Hg(NO3)2]. The yellow form of HgO, on the other hand, can be obtained by precipitating aqueous Hg²⁺ ions with an alkali. Mercury(II) oxide is occasionally utilized in the production of elemental mercury due to its propensity to decompose readily. Upon decomposition, it releases oxygen gas. Historically, in 1774, Joseph Priestley discovered the release of oxygen gas by heating mercuric oxide. However, Priestley did not recognize the gas as oxygen. Instead, he referred to it as dephlogisticated air, in accordance with the phlogiston theory that was prevalent at the time. Later, Antoine Lavoisier identified dephlogisticated air as oxygen, naming it so because of its role in forming acidic compounds. This historical context highlights why the textbook narrative of the discovery of oxygen is somewhat inaccurate, as it is difficult to definitively attribute the discovery to a single individual. Nonetheless, this event marked a significant milestone in the field of chemistry. Additionally, mercury(II) oxide is employed as a material for cathodes in mercury batteries.
